solution: Breaking or weakening of rocks is a natural phenomenon called weathering, and mechanical weathering is the type in which the rock is physically broken into smaller pieces. It is dominant in arid climates. It occurs mainly because of temperature, frost, crystal growth, release of pressure and water. For example, the minerals in a rock expand with heat and contract when the temperature falls, and this continuous expansion and contraction creates tension until cracks develop and the rock breaks; this is common in hot deserts where the diurnal range of temperature is high. Exfoliation, shattering, block disintegration and granular weathering are all forms of mechanical weathering.

The main types of chemical weathering described in the lesson are carbonation, solution and oxidation. In carbonation, rainwater passing through the atmosphere mixes with carbon dioxide and forms dilute carbonic acid (H2O + CO2 = H2CO3), in which materials like limestone dissolve easily. In solution, some minerals of the rock dissolve in water; alkalis in the rock dissolve and make it brittle, and at Wadgaon Darya in Ahmadnagar district limestone is precipitated chemically. In oxidation, the iron present in a rock comes in contact with water and a chemical reaction takes place between iron and oxygen, forming a reddish layer called rust. Water plays an important role in all of these because it is a universal solvent, so chemical weathering is more effective in areas of heavy rainfall. The lesson also says there are many more processes involved in chemical weathering besides these.

Biological weathering occurs because of living organisms. Trees growing on rocks send their roots into them, and as the roots grow bigger they create tension in the rock and start breaking it; pieces of rock get separated in this way. Ants make large anthills, and rats, mice, rabbits and other worms and insects make burrows in the ground. These are called burrowing animals, and weathering of rock occurs because of their activity. Algae, moss, lichen and other flora also grow on rocks and help in weathering.

Weathering is the breaking or weakening of rocks where they lie, and it is of three types: mechanical, chemical and biological. Mass wasting, or mass movement, is the next stage: the weathered rock material starts moving down along the slopes due to gravity and accumulates near the foothills or on the gentler slopes, forming a conical heap. So weathering only breaks or weakens the rock, while mass wasting shifts the already weathered material downslope. In weathering the causes are temperature, water, chemical action and living organisms, whereas in mass wasting the material moves down due to gravity alone. Mass movement is rapid on steeper slopes, as in rockfalls, landslides and land subsidence, and slow on gentle slopes, as in soil creep and solifluction.

False. The lesson says that climate decides which kind of weathering takes place: mechanical weathering is dominant in arid climates while chemical weathering is more effective in humid climates. Earthquakes are not caused by climate; they belong to the internal movements of the earth, and the lesson mentions them only as a cause that can set off rapid mass movements.
Corrected statement: Climate affects weathering.

True. The lesson states that in humid climates chemical weathering is more effective, while mechanical weathering is dominant in arid climates. So mechanical weathering is indeed less effective where the climate is humid.

True. Mechanical weathering is dominant in arid climates. In dry areas the diurnal range of temperature is high, so the minerals in the rocks expand and contract continuously, tension develops, cracks form and the rocks break; this type of weathering is common in the hot deserts.
True. The lesson defines weathering as the breaking or weakening of rocks, which is a natural phenomenon. It can be of three types, mechanical, chemical and biological.

False. Exfoliation is a kind of mechanical weathering. The exposed part of a rock heats more while the inner part stays comparatively cooler, so the outer layers fall apart from the main rock, one after another, just as the skins of an onion can be peeled off. It is a way in which an existing rock is broken, not a way in which a rock is formed.
Corrected statement: Exfoliation is the breaking away of the outer layers of a rock, and it is a type of mechanical weathering.

Weathering process

| Weathering process | Sub-processes |
|---|---|
| Mechanical weathering | Frost ; Exfoliation |
| Chemical weathering | Carbonation ; Solution ; Oxidation |
| Biological weathering | Burrowing by animals ; Breaking of rocks by the growth of roots, algae, moss and lichen |

The three branches of the weathering process are mechanical, chemical and biological weathering. Under mechanical weathering the lesson describes temperature, frost, crystal growth, release of pressure and water, so any one of these fits the blank box beside exfoliation. Under chemical weathering it describes carbonation, solution and oxidation. Under biological weathering it describes the burrowing animals and the growth of roots, algae, moss and lichen on the rocks.
Biological weathering. Ants make large anthills and rats, mice, rabbits and other worms and insects make burrows in the ground. These burrowing animals loosen and break the rock by their activity.

Chemical weathering, by the process of oxidation. The iron present in the rock comes in contact with water and a chemical reaction takes place between iron and oxygen, so a reddish coloured layer called rust forms on the rock. This happens in areas with high rainfall.

Mechanical weathering, by the action of frost. Where temperatures drop below 0 degree C for quite some time, the water collected in the cracks and crevices of the rock freezes and its volume increases. This creates tension in the rock and the rock shatters.

Mechanical weathering, by the action of frost. The volume of water increases when it freezes, so in colder regions the water freezing inside the pipes presses outward and the pipes break. The same increase in volume shatters rocks when water freezes in their cracks and crevices.

Mechanical weathering, caused mainly by temperature. In the hot deserts the diurnal range of temperature is high, so the minerals of the rock expand with heat and contract as the temperature falls. Each mineral reacts differently, so tension develops in the rock particles, cracks form and the rock breaks down into small particles.

Landslides are a kind of rapid mass movement, along with rockfalls and land subsidence, and their effects are very destructive. They are more likely in regions that have a humid climate and steeper slopes. In such regions a thick layer of weathered material forms on the slope; when it rains, the rainwater penetrates this weathered material and its weight increases, and the material then moves very rapidly down the slope. The mudslide at Malin village in Pune district is the example given in the lesson. Sometimes the weathered material does not travel downward but sinks in situ, that is where it is, and this is called slumping. Such rapid mass movements may also be set off by earthquakes.
